opening.headline: When sending the same long front end for each request increases the cost, I understand caching to reuse the front end that has already been processed.
body: Customer-facing services have thousands of tokens of system prompts and tool definitions, and the only thing that changes with each request is a short question from the user. However, each time a request is made, the same first part is sent again, and the model processes the first part anew each time. As a result, the input token cost increases linearly with the number of requests, and the processing time until the first response also increases.

In this class, we'll look at what prompt caching stores and what it reuses, how Gemini, OpenAI, and Claude turn caching on and what minimum conditions they place on it. Learn about the metrics for checking cache hits and when caches are broken, and the criteria for distinguishing requests that have an effective cache from those that do not.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain implicit caching, explicit caching, and minimum token conditions
Cache can distinguish between effective and ineffective requests
This explains why prefixes must match on a token-by-token basis and why cache entries have a lifetime.

screens.title: Send the same long prefix for each request
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare how the same request is handled without and with caching.

visual.alt: A structure in which three requests have the same long front and different questions.

states.label: When there is no caching
states.body: Every customer-facing service request begins with thousands of tokens of system prompts and tool definitions, followed by a short question at the end. The same first part is sent back to each request, and the model processes that first part anew each time. The input token cost increases in proportion to the number of requests, and the first response is delayed by the time it takes to process the first part.

states.label: When there is caching
states.body: If the first part is the same as the previous request, the results that have already been processed can be reused. The model only has to process the new part of the question, reducing both cost and processing time. The key question in this lesson is whether it is possible to reuse the front end that has already been processed without recomputing it.

screens.outro: First, let me recall the first recurring part of my experience.

screens.title: Think about it: repeating front part
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: How many of the prompts I create do not change each time?
items.answer: Role instructions, output formats, tool definitions, and examples are mostly the same for each request. Often, the only things that change are users' questions and recent conversations. The longer the part that does not change, the more effective caching is.

items.prompt: Have you ever had the experience of posting a long document and asking several questions in succession?
items.answer: Each time you paste a document and continue to ask questions about it, the entire document is processed again. The longer the document, the greater the recurring costs. These requests are typical targets for caching.

items.prompt: Imagine the same tool definitions and instructions being carried across all requests.
items.answer: The more tools you have, the longer the definition will be, and that definition will be prepended to the beginning of every request. If a task sends multiple requests, such as an agent, repetitions become more frequent.

screens.outro: Now that we know the scale of the iteration, let's look at what caching stores.

screens.title: Prompt caching and prefix fixation
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to see step-by-step what Prompt Caching stores and under what conditions it is reused.

visual.alt: A structure in which only sections with matching prefixes are reused.
labels: Same content in the same order

steps.title: What do you reuse?
steps.body: Prompt caching reuses intermediate states (KV states) of a model that have already been computed in requests that share the same prefix. A prefix refers to the part that continues from the beginning of the prompt. Since the calculation results from the previous part are rewritten, processing time and cost are reduced accordingly.

steps.title: What is stored is the state
steps.body: What is stored is not the token itself or the previous answer, but the state obtained by processing the previous part. So, if the prefix is ​​the same, it can be reused even if the question is different, and the answer is created anew each time.

steps.title: The entire prefix must match
steps.body: To be reused, all rendered prefixes must match. If anything in the front part is changed, the part behind that point will not be reused. Therefore, the basis of design is to fix the prefix by putting the content that does not change at the front and the questions that change at the end.

steps.title: Claude's prefix order
steps.body: In Claude, cache prefixes are created in the following order: tools, system, messages. Tool definitions come first, system instructions come next, and dialog messages come last. So, if you change the front layer, the cache of the back layer is also affected.

steps.title: New input is still processed
steps.body: The only thing that is reused is the matching front section. New input still needs to be processed. Therefore, the effect of caching increases as the proportion of the reused portion of the total input increases.

screens.outro: Now that we know the principles, let's compare how the three services provide caching.

screens.title: Implicit/explicit caching and minimum token conditions
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn about caching methods and minimum length conditions for each service.

tabs.label: Gemini
tabs.body: In models 2.5 and later, implicit caching is turned on by default, and savings are reflected automatically. Minimum tokens per model are 2,048 or 4,096. Repeated prefixes are automatically applied without any configuration. There is also documentation for directly specifying repeated input with explicit context caching.

tabs.label: OpenAI
tabs.body: It is turned on by default on supported models. The minimum cacheable length varies by model and is 1,024 tokens for GPT-5.6 and later. If requests share a prefix, they'll automatically hit, so you can see the effect without any code changes. There is also a prompt_cache_key value that helps requests that share a common prefix find the same cache.

tabs.label: Claude
tabs.body: Use automatic caching, which places a cache_control at the top of the request, or explicit caching, which places a breakpoint in each block. Automatic caching places a breakpoint at the last cacheable block and moves it forward as the conversation becomes longer. Explicit caching allows you to decide how much to cache. The default lifespan is 5 minutes, and the lifespan is renewed at no additional cost each time it is used. You can also select a 1-hour lifespan.

tabs.label: common rules
tabs.body: Prompts shorter than the minimum length are not cached and no error is generated. So, if you turn on caching and it doesn't have an effect, first make sure your prompt is longer than the minimum length. All three services have a minimum token condition and lifetime, and use metrics to check for hits. When moving services, be sure to double-check that the minimum length and lifetime values ​​are different.

screens.outro: Now that we've checked the conditions, let's check the code where to place the breakpoint.

screens.title: Why prefixes must match token by token from the beginning
screens.lead: Move the slider to see how the reused section changes depending on the changed location of the token. The ten tokens are hypothetical examples to aid understanding.

visual.alt: A bar diagram in which only the front of the changed position among the ten tokens is reused and the back is recalculated.
labels: Recalculate: Because the future has changed
The state of the back token depends on the previous tokens.

stops.body: If the first token changes, all states from 2nd to 10th will be different because they depend on the previous token. There is no section that can be reused, so the saved state cannot be used and all ten are recalculated. This is exactly what happens when you put a value that changes from request to request as the first line of a system instruction.

The state from the 1st to the 4th token remains the same because the contents preceding it are the same. From the 5th to the 10th, the front is different, so 6 are counted again. Even if the back token is literally the same as the previous request, it cannot be reused if the front token has been changed. This is why even if you change just a little bit in the middle of the prompt, everything after that is affected.
If only the last token is different, the 9 states from 1st to 9th are reused and the last one is recalculated. This is why the fixed prefix design, which puts the changing question last, works well.

stops.value: The tokens are the same, only the space is different.
stops.body: Even if the sentence is visually the same, the token string can be different if there is a single space or line break difference. The criterion for matching is not meaning or appearance, but exact matching at the token level. Spaces and line breaks that are automatically added in the template are also subject to inspection.

Even if the first part is exactly the same, the saved state takes up memory and cannot be kept for long. Each service has a fixed retention time (Claude's default lifetime is 5 minutes), so if the request interval is longer than the lifetime, the state is already gone and recalculated from the beginning, with write costs incurred again. Prefix matching and lifetime are two independent conditions for a cache hit.

screens.outro: Now that we know the reasons for matching and longevity, let's read the request structure into code to see where to place breakpoints.

ext.title: Kwon et al., Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention (SOSP 2023, arXiv:2309.06180)

screens.title: Cache hit metrics and cache invalidation
screens.lead: Read the request structure below to find out where Claude places explicit breakpoints and what values it checks for hits. The explanation on the right also describes symptoms when the position is incorrectly positioned.

notes.note: Place cache_control in an unchanging instruction block. The breakpoint records the prefix up to this block as one cache entry. If you want a longer lifespan, you can specify 1h for ttl.

Blocks that change from request to request, such as time, are placed after a breakpoint. If you place a breakpoint in this block, the prefix will be different each time, so there is nothing to read, just write every time. Breakpoints should be placed in the same last block between requests.

Leave questions last. In the response's usage, cache_creation_input_tokens is the number of newly written tokens, and cache_read_input_tokens is the number of tokens read from the cache. If both are 0, it is not cached and is most likely below the minimum length.

Changing the tool definition will invalidate the tools, system, and messages caches. Changing one level invalidates that level and subsequent levels, and changing thinking settings or effort invalidates the message cache. Gemini checks for hits with usage.total_cached_tokens, and OpenAI checks for hits with cached_tokens.

screens.outro: Now that you know the indicators and invalidation conditions, let's solve the service case step by step.

screens.title: Explanatory example: Service with long system prompts and only changing questions
screens.lead: The instructor explains the case step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: There is a support service that provides thousands of tokens worth of system prompts and tool definitions followed by short user questions. We receive tens of thousands of requests for the same rescue every day. The question part varies from request to request, but the first part is always the same.

steps.title: Step 1: The first request creates the cache
steps.body: The first request processes the prefix and writes it to the cache. Depending on the service, write fees may apply. This request may cost the same or slightly more than without caching, but subsequent requests make it back.

steps.title: Step 2: Afterwards the request is read
steps.body: Next requests will read from the cache because they match the same prefix. It is calculated as a read unit cost and the front processing time is also reduced. Users receive a faster first response, and services have reduced input costs.

steps.title: Step 3: Recalculate only the question
steps.body: Only the question portion is recalculated, so the more requests you make, the greater the savings. As requests continue within the lifetime, the lifetime is renewed to maintain the cache. A service with steady traffic is more advantageous.

steps.title: Step 4: The amount of savings is determined by the unit price list.
steps.body: The actual savings will depend on the cache read and write costs in the price table for each model. After checking the rate in the pricing document, calculate the P&L based on the number of requests and prefix length. If requests are infrequent and never reused, writing costs can only increase.

steps.title: OK
steps.body: Effectiveness is directly verified by indicators of response. If cached_tokens or cache_read_input_tokens is equal to the length of the prefix, it is a hit. If the index is 0, three things are checked in order: minimum length, prefix match, and lifetime. This order is the one that will most quickly narrow down the cause.

steps.title: organizing
steps.body: The benefit of caching in this service is greatest when the prefix is long, requests are steady, and the front end is stable. If any of the three conditions weaken, the effectiveness will diminish, so keep an eye on the indicators.

screens.outro: Now that we've seen cases where it works, let's tabulate cases where it doesn't work.

data.notes: Improvements have three things in common: Moving the changing value back, checking the call interval or lifetime settings according to the lifetime, and checking the hit with an indicator. Caching isn't just something you turn on; it requires design and measurement. The last two rows of the table are representative of unintentional prefix practice, so keep an eye on them when reviewing your code. Don't forget to check your metrics again after making improvements.

screens.title: Key takeaway: Select a sentence and check the evidence
screens.lead: If you select each summary sentence, the evidence will unfold. There is nothing to enter or submit.

items.prompt: Prompt caching reuses computational state for the same prefix
items.answer: What is stored is not the token or the answer, but the state obtained by processing the previous part. New input is still processed, so only the leading part of the match is reused.

items.prompt: Fix content that does not change at the front and place content that changes at the back.
items.answer: Since the entire prefix must match to be reused, the time, request ID, and user question are left behind. Claude puts breakpoints in the same last block between requests. If you put a breakpoint on a changing block, it will just be written every time.

items.prompt: All three companies have minimum token conditions and lifespans and confirm hits with indicators.
items.answer: Gemini and OpenAI are turned on by default, and Claude is turned on with cache_control. If it's shorter than the minimum length, it won't be cached and you won't get an error, so you should check it as an indicator.

items.prompt: Changing tools, systems, or settings can lead to cache invalidation.
items.answer: In Claude, a change at one level invalidates the cache at that level and subsequent levels. Any changes to the tool definition will be invalidated, so keep the front layer stable. The more requests there are and the longer the prefix, the more valuable this reliability becomes.

screens.outro: Lastly, let's think about it in relation to our own work.

screens.title: Connect to my work
screens.lead: This screen is for reading only. Read the questions and think for yourself. You will not enter or submit an answer.

paragraphs: Key terms in this lesson are prompt caching, context caching, prefix pinning, and cache hit metrics. Let's go back to the original question. Can the previously processed portion be reused without recalculating it? The answer is yes, if the first part matches from request to request, exceeds the minimum length, and is reused within its lifetime.
Read my prompt from top to bottom and indicate where the changing values are. If the time, request ID, and username are in the front, simply moving them to the back may work.

Next, look at the metrics of the response. Making sure the number of tokens you hit is close to the prefix length will help you know if your design is working as intended. If the metric is 0, we suspect the minimum length, then the prefix match, and then the lifetime.
Lastly, remember that the amount of savings depends on the cache read and write costs in the price table for each model. Caching is not always beneficial if there are not enough requests.

callout.label: Questions to Think About
callout.text: Where does prompt caching get stuck in my business? Think about where in your prompt the value that changes with each request is at the very beginning.

checks.q: What is the appropriate condition for prompt caching to be reused and its effect?
options: The question must be the same because the text of the previous answer to the same question is returned as is.
Since the input token itself is stored, it is reused if the number of tokens is the same.
Since the intermediate state of the model obtained by processing the previous part is reused, the entire prefix must match.
If the request has similar meaning, the intermediate state is reused even if the prefix is different.
checks.explain: What is stored is not the token, but the state obtained by processing the previous part. Since the entire rendered prefix must match, the content that does not change is placed first, and the questions that change are placed at the end.

wrong.0: This is not a way to reuse answers. New input is still processed.
wrong.1: What is stored is not the token itself, but its processed state.
wrong.3: The condition is prefix agreement, not semantic similarity.

checks.intro: See what prompt caching stores and when it takes effect.
checks.correctFeedback: That's right. What is stored is the previous part processed, so the entire prefix must match to be reused.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The cache does not store the answers or tokens themselves, nor are they reused for similarity in meaning. Remember that the prefix must match literally.

checks.q: Claude changed some of the tool definitions between requests. What is the effect on cache?
options: Only the changed tool definition portion is processed anew and the rest of the cache remains the same.
Tool definitions are not cached and therefore have no effect.
Only the messages cache is invalidated and the system cache is maintained.
Since this is a tools-level change, all tools·system·messages caches are invalidated.
checks.explain: Cache prefixes are created in the order tools → system → messages, and changes at one level invalidate that level and subsequent levels. Since tools comes first, everything is invalid.

wrong.0: If the prefix changes, anything after that point will not be reused.
wrong.1: Tool definitions are included at the beginning of the prefix.
wrong.2: When tools are changed, the system at the next level also becomes invalid.

checks.intro: Calculate what extent of the cache is affected by changing the tool definition.
checks.correctFeedback: That's right. Since the prefix is ​​created in the order of tools, system, and messages, changes to the first tools are invalidated at all subsequent levels.
checks.incorrectFeedback: It's easy to think that only the changed parts are updated, but the prefix continues from the beginning. When one level changes, it and the levels after it become invalid as well.

checks.q: Pair caching effects and responses with the following request situations:
left: Short prompts that fall short of the minimum length
There is a request ID at the beginning that changes for each request.
Requests with the same prefix rarely come past their lifetime
Long common instructions are repeated and only the questions change.
right: Since the prefixes do not match and will not be reused, the changing values are moved to the back.
The greater the caching effect and the more requests, the greater the savings.
Since the effectiveness is low due to the end of the lifespan, check the call interval or lifespan settings.
checks.explain: The cache depends on three conditions: minimum length, prefix matching, and lifetime. Check hits with indicators and find out which conditions were broken.
checks.intro: Match the conditions that influence caching effectiveness by situation.
checks.correctFeedback: That's correct. You diagnosed appropriately for each situation which of the three conditions - minimum length, prefix matching, and lifetime - was broken.
checks.incorrectFeedback: There is a mismatched pair. Try to distinguish between cases that are short and not cached, cases that do not match because the first part has changed, and cases that have expired, and connect each correspondence.

glossary.def: This is a function that reduces cost and delay by reusing the previous calculation state that has already been processed in requests with the same prefix.
In terms from the Gemini documentation, this is a feature that utilizes a cache of repeated input tokens. Models after 2.5 have implicit caching by default.

The design maintains cache consistency by placing content that does not change before the prompt and content that does change after it. This is because only the parts that matched on a token-by-token basis are reused.
Like cached_tokens in response usage, this is a field that tells the number of tokens read from the cache.
The prefix changes and the saved state can no longer be used. The changed floor and subsequent floors are invalid.

misconceptions.myth: Turning on caching makes all requests cheaper.
misconceptions.fact: It will only hit if it is greater than or equal to the minimum length and the prefix matches. The short prompt is not cached and does not produce an error.

misconceptions.myth: The response sentence is stored in the cache.
misconceptions.fact: What is stored is the state obtained from the previous processing. The response is generated new for each request.

misconceptions.myth: It is okay to put the current time at the beginning of the prompt.
misconceptions.fact: If there is a value in front that changes from request to request, the prefix will not match and the cache will be broken. Leave the changing values ​​behind.

misconceptions.myth: If you just change the middle of the prompt a little, the cache at the beginning will remain the same.
misconceptions.fact: The state of one token depends on all tokens before it. Since all states behind the point where it was fixed are different, they are not reused, and only the front is maintained.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: Prompt caching reuses computational state for the same prefix.
Fix content that does not change at the front and place content that does change at the back.
All three services have a minimum token condition and lifetime, and use metrics to check for hits.
Changing tools, systems, or settings can lead to cache invalidation.
